list.listitem: Typically, herpes zoster (HZ) is characterized by unilateral dermatomal pain and rash.C
Initiating treatment within 72 hours with appropriate antivirals will significantly decrease the incidence of acute pain but does not decrease the frequency of postherpetic neuralgia (PHN).A
Amitriptyline treatment within 48 hours reduces the risk of persistent pain at six months in patients older than 60 years.B
Corticosteroids do not improve long-term outcomes.B
Herpes zoster vaccine administered to patients age 50 and older, who are not immunocompromised, decreases the incidence of herpes zoster and subsequent postherpetic neuralgia.A

background.definition: Herpes zoster, better known as “shingles,” is the reactivation of a latent varicella zoster-virus infection from within the sensory ganglia, resulting in pain and rash in a dermatomal distribution.

list.listitem: Overall: 1.5-3.0/1000/year (0.15%-0.3% per year).
Approximately 300,000 to 600,000 new cases per year.
Lifetime risk: 10% to 20%.
HZ equally affects males and females; blacks are one-fourth as likely to be affected as whites.
Thirty percent of infections occur in persons older than 50 years.
Over 75 years old: 10/1000/year (1% per year).
Higher incidence in immunocompromised individuals.
HIV-infected persons: 29.4/1000/year (3% per year).
The incidence increased among US veterans older than 40 years from an annual incidence of 3.10 episodes per 1000 veterans in 2000 to 5.22 in 2007.
Herpes zoster virus (VZV).
The reactivation of varicella-zoster virus infection caused clinically relevant herpes-zoster.
During the latent period, the virus expresses only minimal proteins (as few as five) in neurons and satellite cells.

If a person's cell-mediated immunity is sufficiently strong against those proteins, particularly immediate-early protein 63, the infection's reactivation is avoided. When immunity to the proteins wanes, reactivation occurs.
During reactivation, inflammation and possibly hemorrhagic necrosis of the dorsal spinal ganglion leads to pain and subsequent rash along the dermatomal distribution in question.

A person cannot contract shingles from another individual. Individuals exposed to the varicella-zoster virus for the first time will develop chickenpox (varicella) and not shingles because they have no latent virus to reactivate at that point.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Immunocompromise with impaired cell-mediated immunity (HIV, transplant patients)
Chronic respiratory diseases (asthma, chronic obstructive lung disease)
Physical trauma to the affected area

list.listitem: All patients age 50 and older who are not immunosuppressed should have zoster vaccine.A
Zoster vaccine should be given to all patients age 19 and older that have immunodeficiency or will be immunosuppressed from disease or immunotherapy and are at risk for HZ.A
Zoster vaccine reduces the incidence of herpes zoster (number needed to treat (NNT) = 50 at three years).A
Pre-vaccination screening for a history of chickenpox is not needed. In patients with a negative VZV serology, one should follow the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) guideline.
Zoster vaccine is not associated with an increased risk of herpes zoster infection in patients with immune-mediated diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel disease.
Zoster vaccine should be avoided during pregnancy.
The older herpes zoster vaccine (Zostavax) is strongly associated with a lower risk of dementia. This association has been shown with the newer vaccine also.

RZV is more effective against HZV infection and PHN than the live Zoster vaccine (Zoster Vaccine Live, ZVL, Zostavax). ZVL's effectiveness declined sharply, while RZV declined modestly four years after vaccination. RZV is preferred over ZVL (which is no longer marketed in the US). The long-term effectiveness of two doses of RZV is significantly more than one dose of RZV (76% vs 64%).
RZV may be given to patients who had HZ or received ZVL in the past. According to expert opinion, RZV should be administered >2 months after ZVL.
A systematic review of 7 RCTs found that RZV was also effective in immunocompromised individuals. The reduction in HZ incidence was 81% (RR 0.19, 95% CI 0.09-0.44).

RZV causes more injection site pain. Both doses of RZV are required to achieve an adequate immune response. One cannot predict if those patients who experienced injection site pain from the first RZV will experience it again with the second dose. Some patients who experienced side effects from the first dose may refuse the second dose.

Post-marketing Medicare claims observational data showed that within 42 days after the RZV vaccine, there was an increased risk for Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) with six cases per million dose administered with the first dose and no increased risk with the second dose.(RZV package insert) In the United States, the incidence of patients hospitalized with GBS ranged from 1.65 to 1.79 per 100,000 in 2008.

A retrospective cohort study found that in the Medicare Advantage population with a history of herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO), the risk of recurrence of HZO post RZV is higher than in the unvaccinated population.
RZV is more cost-effective than most adult vaccines and more cost-effective than ZVL. RZV is safe in frail elderly as well.

listitem.strong: Live Zoster Vaccine (Zoster Vaccine Live, ZVL, Zovarax)

list.listitem: In 2020, ZVL was removed from the market and is no longer available in the United States.
ZVL was recommended by ACIP for use in immunocompetent patients aged >60 years.
In patients aged >60 years, ZVL decreases the incidence of HZ by 51.3%, reduces the occurrence of PHN by 66.5%, and the burden of illness from HZ by 61.1%.
VZL is contraindicated in patients with immunodeficiency or immunosuppressed.

In patients with a history of herpes zoster, the ACIP recommends zoster vaccination but has no recommendation on timing. Some international immunization advisory committees recommend waiting at least one year before zoster vaccination. Lee et al. showed ZVL given at 6 to 12 months, 1 to 3 years, and > three years post HZ did not result in a significant difference in humoral and cellular immunity.
Unilateral dermatomal pain preceding a rash occurs in 75% of patients.C
The rash will be vesicular and unilateral, typically in one or two neighboring dermatomes; it is most commonly in a thoracic or lumbar dermatome.C
Diagnostic testing is not recommended; herpes zoster is a clinical diagnosis.C

The pain of acute neuritis from HZ may be constant or intermittent and may present days to weeks before the development of a rash. The patient may experience tingling, itchy, burning, throbbing, and stabbing sensations. Allodynia or hyperalgesia may also be present from history and during the examination. Some patients have HZ but no rash, this phenomenon is called zoster sine herpete.

Seventy-five percent of patients will have pain before the development of any rash. The pain is typically located in a unilateral dermatomal distribution, followed by the eruption of clusters of maculopapular and then vesiculopustular rash over an erythematous base.
The rash may be present in one or two neighboring dermatomes. In 7 to 10 days, the rash usually crusts and becomes dry.
Thoracic and lumbar dermatomes are the most commonly involved sites.
Less than 20% of people complain of fatigue or fever.
Some lesions may occasionally be present outside of the dermatome secondary to the hematogenous spread of the virus.
HZ is a clinical diagnosis, and diagnostic tests are not routinely recommended.

If the diagnosis is in question, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing, or viral culture for VZV is recommended. PCR is the most sensitive and specific test. DFA and viral culture require collecting a specimen from scraping the surface of unroofed vesicles.
See algorithm in .
Patients at increased risk and aware of the potential complications from HZ infection will be more willing to receive the vaccine.
Education on the effectiveness, safety, insurance coverage, and recommendation by a clinician will increase the patient's willingness to get the HZV vaccine from 49% to 75%.
Valacyclovir, famciclovir, or acyclovir should be started within 72 hours of symptom onset in patients older than 50.A
Options for pain control in the acute setting include gabapentin, tramadol, NSAIDs, and tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs).B
Amitriptyline (25 mg daily for 90 days) initiated within 48 hours reduces the incidence of persistent pain at six months in patients older than 60 years.B
Postherpetic neuralgia can be treated with TCAs, gabapentin, pregabalin, opioids, and even intrathecal corticosteroids.B

Antivirals have been shown to decrease the duration and number of lesions and the severity of pain from acute neuritis and stop viral shedding. Antivirals may reduce pain in the acute setting. Still, other agents may be needed for complete pain relief.

Antivirals have a better effect on individuals older than 50 for HZV infection. Patients younger than 50 should be given antiviral therapy on a case-by-case basis, depending on the severity of illness and comorbidities.

Antiviral therapy should be initiated within 72 hours of the onset of symptoms. After 72 hours, antiviral treatment should be started for all immunocompromised patients and if there are new, none crusted lesions or complications.

Oral valacyclovir (1000 mg three times daily (tid)) and oral famciclovir (500 mg tid) are superior to oral acyclovir (800 mg five times daily). Acyclovir has lower oral bioavailability and decreased antiviral activities. Treatment should be for seven days with valacyclovir and famciclovir; 7 to 10 days with acyclovir. Depending on the complication, consider intravenous antiviral therapy.
In patients who cannot afford newer antivirals such as famciclovir or valacyclovir, acyclovir is a reasonable choice.

Acyclovir and famciclovir do not decrease the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia; there are insufficient data on other newer antiviral agents.There is some evidence that antivirals may reduce the amount of pain in patients with postherpetic neuralgia.

When used, corticosteroids need to be administered with antiviral therapy. Adding corticosteroids to the treatment plan shows only modest benefits in the early crusting of lesions, reduction of acute pain, and improved activities of daily living.

A systematic review identified 11 case reports of steroids for herpes zoster ophthalmicus, with no clear difference in outcomes between patients receiving antivirals only compared with those receiving combination therapy.
Adding steroids confers no benefit in the prevention of postherpetic neuralgia.B
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), acetaminophen, and tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are beneficial in managing pain in the acute setting.
5% lidocaine patch applied bid to intact skin with acute allodynia from HZ resulted in decreased pain compared to the vehicle (placebo) patch.

Topical capsaicin can be considered for neuropathic pain. In a Cochrane review of 6 trials (389 participants in total) comparing the regular application of low dose (0.075%) capsaicin cream with placebo cream; the NNT for any pain relief over six to eight weeks was 6.6 (4.1-17).
Amitriptyline 25 mg nightly for 90 days, started in patients aged 60 and older, within 48 hours of rash onset reduced the risk of postherpetic neuralgia.
Gabapentin, in one study, has been shown to lessen the pain in the acute setting when given as a single dose of 900 mg.
Pregabalin is effective in treating symptoms of postherpetic neuralgia (NNT = 5 to achieve at least a 50% improvement in symptoms).
In a small cross-over study, the combination of gabapentin and nortriptyline appeared more effective in treatment-naive patients than either drug alone.

A systematic review identified 6 RCTs with 292 patients comparing gabapentin (n=118) or pregabalin (n=37) with placebo. Studies were at high risk of bias and high heterogeneity. Possible reduction of pain with gabapentin was seen at 4 weeks but not 1 and 2 weeks.
Oxycodone are more effective than placebo or gabapentin for pain in the acute setting of HZ.

In patients with severe pain from HZ acute neuritis, a randomized controlled trial (RCT) showed acupuncture provide significant and comparable pain relief when compared to patients treated with pregabalin (75-600 mg/day), local anesthesia (peridural neural blockage in those with lumbar or sacral involvement; or perineural peripheral blockade), and opioid (transdermal buprenorphine 35-90 mcg/h or oral oxycodone 50-400 mg daily) combined.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCT showed that acupuncture combined with moxibustion decreased pain intensity compared to pharmacotherapy, but the authors were unable to establish clinical significance.

In a retrospective cohort study, dexamethasone 5mg and 3 ml of 0.18% ropivacine, when administered within 12 weeks of HZ infection via TFESI, can decrease pain by targeting the affected nerve root and dorsal spinal ganglion. This study was limited to three months follow-up.
Depending on the severity and extent of the complication from HZV infection, consider referral or hospitalization.
The most common complication from HZ is PHN. Depending on the source, one defined PHN as residual pain in the affected dermatome at 30 days or more.
More than 50% of cases of PHN are in patients over the age of 50 years.

PEER systemic review of randomized controlled trials in patients with PHN, diabetic neuropathy, and trigeminal neuralgia showed moderate success with anticonvulsants and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs). There was inadequate clinical evidence for pain control with capsaicin, scant evidence for pain relief with tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), and very low-quality evidence on the effectiveness of acupuncture.

Anticonvulsants (gabapentin and pregabalin) were helpful in patients with chronic neuropathic conditions, with an NNT of 7 (95% CI 1.45 TO 1.63). In a Cochrane review of gabapentin for chronic pain, including two PHN trials, the NNT for effective pain relief in PHN was 3.9 (95% CI, 3.0-5.7). Another Cochrane review found the pregabalin 300-600 mg daily dose to have the best (lowest) number needed to treat for an additional beneficial (NNTB) outcome with at least 30% pain relief compared to placebo in patients with PHN. At these doses, somnolence occurred in 16% to 25%, and dizziness occurred in 29% to 35%.
SNRIs (duloxetine, venlafaxine, or desvenlafaxine), compared to placebo, NNT was 7 (95% CI 1.33 to 1.59).
There is no good quality or long-term randomized controlled trial using tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs).

8% high-concentration topical capsaicin applied to the affected area in the clinic may result in moderate pain relief in a small number of patients with PHN. Though, RCTs did not show a difference between low or high potency treatment.
Topical lidocaine may provide pain relief in some patients. Depending on the regional cost of the treatment, it may be more cost-effective than other options.

Intrathecal methylprednisolone reduces pain from postherpetic neuralgia. Due to the invasive nature and potentially serious complications, it should be reserved for those patients not responsive to other modalities.

A phase 3 trial randomized patients with post-herpetic neuralgia to crisugabalin 20 mg twice daily, 40 mg twice daily, or placebo for 12 weeks. Changes in an 11 point symptom scorewere greater for the 40 mg (-2.2 points) and 80 mg (-2.6 points) than placebo (-1.1 points). This difference was statistically significant but is of uncertain clinical significance.
Patients with eye involvement, such as HZO, should be referred to an ophthalmologist.
Standard treatment is valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily for 7 to 14 days, initiated within 72 hours of the onset of symptoms.

A systematic review identified 11 case reports of steroids for herpes zoster ophthalmicus, with no clear difference in outcomes between patients receiving antivirals only compared with those receiving combination therapy.
Patients diagnosed with herpes zoster ophthalmicus were found to have a 4.5-fold (95% CI, 2.4-8.3) higher risk of stroke than the matched comparison cohort.
Case reports have reported use of systemic corticosteroids in patients with HZO but clinical trials are lacking.
Predictors of recurrence of HZO include the presence of immunosuppression, a higher initial intraocular pressure, uveitis, and involvement of the cornea.
Most patients, whether treated or not, will recover completely: the lesions will gradually crust and fade over a 5- to 10-day period, and pain will subside within one month.C
Postherpetic neuralgia is unpredictable but occurs more frequently in older individuals, particularly those not treated with antivirals.C

Treatment with antivirals, if initiated within 72 hours, does not reduce the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia. However, there is some evidence that it may reduce pain in patients with postherpetic neuralgia.B

A study of 94 immunocompetent patients with herpes zoster and pain of at least 20 on a scale of 0 to 100 followed them for six months. While half reported at least some pain at three months, and 32% still reported pain at six months, the average pain report was 11 on the 100-point scale. Only 3% of patients reported “clinically relevant pain” at three months, and only 2% scored at least three on the 100-point scale at six months.

In patients with a previous episode of herpes zoster, 1.2-9.6% experienced a recurrence. Recurrence was more common in females, younger patients, immunocompromized persons, comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, chronic obstructive lung disease, chronic kideny disease) and those with a family history.

All patients over age 50 should be treated with antivirals, given no contraindications to the medication, as long as patients are within the 72-hour window or if they are beyond the 72-hour window, and new lesions or complications are present.

One RCT of patients older than 60 years with shingles compared 25 mg amitriptyline initiated within 48 hours of the rash onset and continued for 90 days with a placebo. The amitriptyline group showed a 50% decrease in pain prevalence at six months (NNT = 5).
Pregnant women should avoid exposure to HZ or varicella if they are not immune.

In a population-based historical cohort study of 837,795 live-born infants in Denmark, exposure to acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir in the first trimester (N = 1804 pregnancies) was not associated with an increased risk of major birth defects.
HZ is much less common in children.
Diagnosis is the same, but treatment may not be necessary other than acute pain relief.
